narrative:
The model gives you a 32.0% estimated chance of failing your final year—roughly one in three. That is not a certainty, but it is a meaningful risk, and it is why the model’s decision is that you must take remedial courses rather than proceed without support.

The strongest reason is your history of past class failures: you have three, while students who passed have an average of zero. This was the top feature and it pushed the prediction toward failing more than any other factor. The next two most influential factors actually worked in your favor. Your father’s occupation being at home, which is uncommon among passers, and your guardian being someone other than a mother or father, also uncommon, both pushed the prediction toward passing. They softened, but did not overturn, the concern created by your failure history. Other parts of your profile, such as not wanting higher education, no home internet, high weekend alcohol use, very high free time, and frequent going out, add context for why support is important.

To improve your chances, treat the remedial courses as a way to break the pattern of past failures. Use them to build a weekly study routine, seek extra help before problems accumulate, reduce weekend drinking and going-out time, and arrange reliable internet access. Also consider setting a goal of continuing to higher education, since every passing student in the comparison group wanted that.
